title: Hash cons a toy node

samples.label: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "x" [] in string_of_bool (a == b)

samples.expr: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "y" [] in Printf.sprintf "%d %d" a.id b.id
samples.label: let mk = create () in let a = mk "x" [] in let b = mk "y" [] in Printf.sprintf "%d %d" a.id b.id

hints: The shape: `let create () = let tbl = Hashtbl.create 16 in let next = ref 0 in fun op src -> ...`. A function can return a function, and the one it returns still sees `tbl` and `next`.
Keep a `Hashtbl` and an id counter inside `create`, so each call gets its own. The key is the op plus the ids of the sources, because sources are already hash consed.
On a hit, return the stored node itself, not a copy, so `==` holds. Only bump the counter when you actually build a new node.

answer.code:
type node = { id : int; op : string; src : node list }

let create () =
  let tbl = Hashtbl.create 64 and next = ref 0 in
  fun op src ->
    let key = (op, List.map (fun n -> n.id) src) in
    match Hashtbl.find_opt tbl key with
    | Some n -> n
    | None -> let n = { id = !next; op; src } in incr next; Hashtbl.add tbl key n; n
answer.explain: Each `create ()` makes its own table and counter, so tables never share ids. The key `(op, source ids)` is enough because the sources were themselves hash consed: equal sources already have equal ids. Returning the stored record on a hit is what makes `make` give back the physically same node.
